paper_title: SpatialBrain: Spatial Intelligence Growing from Experience

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Spatial reasoning requires more than access to geometric tools: a reasoner must decide when direct observation is sufficient and when to reconstruct, measure, or change reference frames. We present SpatialBrain, a framework that retains experience about these decisions while keeping its vision-language backbone fixed. The key distinction is between evidence about a scene and experience about how to reason with that evidence. 3DFusionMemory fuses current-scene observations into queryable spatial relations. A Spatial Skill Library provides reusable tool procedures, and Spatial Cognition associates task conditions with experience about when and how to use memory and skills. Completed trajectories are abstracted into process records and consolidated between task blocks, allowing later decisions to draw on earlier execution without transferring scene coordinates or reference answers. Across five spatial-reasoning benchmarks, SpatialBrain improves on direct answers from the same backbone on four and ties on the fifth. Component comparisons, experience-coverage curves, and traced resource decisions characterize how the framework accumulates and uses these resources.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: The same visual scene can pose very different reasoning problems. visible attribute may be read directly, an object-relative direction requires reference frame, and distance estimate may require geometric evidence from several views. Route questions additionally require keeping track of successive movements. Spatial benchmarks expose these differences through multi-image reasoning, limited-view scene construction, dynamic spatial aptitude, and degraded observations [12, 19, 24, 28, 33]. useful reasoner must therefore choose the computation as well as produce the answer. Reconstructing every scene can add unnecessary cost and noisy evidence, while answering directly can overlook information that must be integrated across views. Spatial representations learned through training [4, 6] and tools for perception, reconstruction, and simulation [5, 7, 17, 35] expand the computations available to reasoner. Agent methods also retain reflections and reusable workflows from earlier tasks [21, 23, 25, 32]. Access to resource, however, does not specify when it is useful. procedure for computing relative directions can be reused across scenes; the coordinates on which it previously operated cannot. The challenge is to retain experience that informs resource use while grounding each answer in the current scene. SpatialBrain separates scene evidence, reusable computation, and experience about resource use. It operates 1 Figure 1 SpatialBrain: spatial reasoning with experience reuse. Spatial Cognition chooses how to use direct reasoning, spatial skills, and scene evidence. Completed trajectories update procedures and resource-use experience for later tasks; 3DFusionMemory is rebuilt for each scene. The scene is illustrative. as an agent: vision-language reasoner that can select and call tools. After completing tasks, it retains abstract records of the conditions encountered, resources used, and execution feedback. Later tasks consult these records to choose reasoning route, memory-access mode, or skill. We call this cross-task adaptation self-evolution. The model weights remain fixed; the external experience available to the controller changes. Unlike correcting an answer within one task, self-evolution changes the state available to subsequent tasks. Our core contributions address three parts of this reasoning process (Figure 1): 3DFusionMemory grounds reasoning in shared scene state by fusing object, pose, camera, and route observations into queryable spatial evidence with supporting views and uncertainty. Spatial Skill Library makes recurring spatial computations reusable through parameterized tool procedures, separating the operation from the scene-specific inputs on which it acts. Spatial Cognition accumulates condition-specific experience about when and how to use memory and skills. Past process feedback and costs inform resource selection, connecting completed trajectories to later reasoning decisions. Tasks within block share prior experience and maintain separate scene memories. Updates occur after the block finishes, without reference answers. Evaluation with GPT-5.6-sol shows improvements over direct answers on four of five benchmarks and tie on the fifth. Component comparisons and execution traces examine resource use and how earlier experience changes later decisions.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Spatial intelligence. SpatialVLM and SpatialRGPT develop spatial representations through targeted supervision [4, 6], while Thinking in Space studies cognitive maps for video reasoning [27]. Tool-based 2 approaches expose visual programs, geometric constraints, stateful computation, and simulation to reasoner [5, 7, 11, 17, 35]. Structured representations include S-Agents scene and agent memories and AlloSpatials allocentric maps [8, 20]. SpatialCLI provides specialist tools, and SATURN and OmniView-Space emphasize perspective-aware reasoning [13, 16, 34]. SpatialBrain uses execution experience to decide when and how to invoke spatial representations and computations. Agent skills and memory. Executable skills and recurring workflows provide reusable computation, as in Voyager and Agent Workflow Memory [23, 25]. Skill-3D distills scene-aware tool workflows and failure lessons from rollouts for skill-guided inference and agentic post-training [14]. SpatialBrain focuses on blockwise, reference-label-free test-time resource adaptation with fixed model weights, separating currentscene geometry from persistent resource-use experience. Episodic reflection and linked memory notes retain broader experience [18, 26], whereas object-centric scene graphs and exploration snapshots retain spatial evidence [9, 29]. In SpatialBrain, the Skill Library stores how to execute procedure, strategic experience records when and how to use it, and 3DFusionMemory represents what the current scene supports. Self-evolving agents. Self-evolving agents differ in what they update. Reflexion retains verbal feedback for subsequent trials [21], while ExpeL distills experience from training tasks for later inference [32]. Agentic Context Engineering consolidates contextual playbooks through generation, reflection, and curation [31]. Automated Design of Agentic Systems searches agent programs using an expanding archive [10], while the Darwin Godel Machine modifies and tests agent code [30]. SpatialBrain updates external spatial strategies and procedural records from completed test-time trajectories.

sections.title: 3.1 Overview
sections.content: Given images I1:K, question q, and optional answer choices O, SpatialBrain solves task xi = (I1:K, q, O) using fixed vision-language backbone and perception and geometry tools. Spatial Cognition selects the reasoning route and access to memory and skills. Tool observations populate the scene memory, and skills carry out reusable computations on the current inputs. An execution trajectory records these decisions, calls, returned evidence, and process checks. Completed trajectories supply experience for later tasks without updating model weights, as illustrated in Figure 2. This separation gives two timescales of state: scene evidence changes within task, while experience about using evidence changes between task blocks. Let index tasks, within-task execution step, and block. The state available to the reasoner is Si,t = (Gi,t, Hb), Hb = (Lb, Pb). (1) Here Gi,t is the current scene graph, Lb the skill library, and Pb the strategic experience used by Spatial Cognition. Observations update Gi,t during execution; all tasks in block read the same committed snapshot Hb and keep separate scene graphs. procedure for comparing object-relative directions can thus persist without carrying its earlier object coordinates into new scene. 3.2 3DFusionMemory Different views expose different objects and different sides of the same object. 3DFusionMemory fuses these observations into shared scene frame, where object identities connect evidence across views and spatial relations connect objects. The memory for the current task is Gi,t = (Vi,t, Ei,t, Ci,t, Ri,t), (2) where Vi,t contains object nodes, Ei,t spatial relations, Ci,t camera states, and Ri,t ordered route history. Nodes retain detections, 3D centers, available point sets and extents, pose, semantic axes, and supporting views. Depth and camera poses place observations in the scene frame; matched observations update an 3 Figure 2 Self-evolution from earlier trajectories. (a) Initial reasoning leaves the reference frame unresolved. (b) Completed earlier trajectories are abstracted and consolidated between task blocks. (c) Accumulated experience guides memory access and skill selection for the same target. The trajectories and outcomes are illustrative. objects center through confidence-weighted fusion (Appendix D). Repeated observations support the same node, while complementary views add objects that single view does not cover. Relations are then computed between these fused object representations (Figure 3). Queries return distances and cameraor object-frame relations together with confidence, supporting views, and ambiguity. Ordered route state supports successive translations and rotations. The planner may receive compact spatial facts, or memory may be reserved for answer checking. Skills and reasoning steps can therefore refer to the same grounded objects instead of reconstructing their relations independently.

sections.title: 3.3 Spatial Skill Library
sections.content: Recurring spatial operations can reuse computation even when the objects and images change. The library represents each skill as procedure with an explicit applicability condition and inputoutput interface: ℓ = (Aℓ, Xℓ, Pℓ, Yℓ), ℓ Lb. (3) In equation 3, Aℓ specifies applicability, Xℓ typed input requirements, Pℓ parameterized tool procedure, and Yℓ its returned evidence. For example, relative-direction procedure binds reference frame before computing displacement. Its parameters refer to the current tasks objects, so the same procedure can operate on different scenes. Seed skills initialize the library. Completed trajectories add recurring execution patterns and records of their use. Spatial Cognition can withhold skill, expose it as planning hint, or permit execution. sections.title: 3.4 Spatial Cognition
sections.content: Deciding when and how to use resources. Spatial Cognition turns execution experience into conditional resource decisions. Its strategic store associates input-visible task conditions with past resource choices, process checks, failures, and costs. task signature σi describes the reference frame, relation scope, output form, temporal structure, metric demand, and view count. It uses neither reference answers nor benchmark category labels. Given this signature and the available experience, the controller selects gi = π(σi; Pb, Lb) = (ri, mi, Ki, νi). (4) Here ri chooses direct-first or tool-assisted reasoning, mi controls memory access (off, answer-checking only, or planner-visible), Ki Lb gives permitted skills, and νi specifies verification and revision. Equation 4 is resource selection, not answer prediction. skills how describes computation; Cognitions how describes how to use that computation and its evidence. The controller combines initial rules with stored experience rather than training an additional model. Resource changes require supporting experience. In the executable configuration, route and memory alternatives must have sufficient historical support, acceptable process risk, and lower estimated token cost; otherwise the default remains. At most one learned route or memory factor changes per request. Skill selection requires compatible inputs and availability, while verification and resource limits follow fixed rules. Appendix specifies these conditions. Process feedback is not correctness reward: it describes execution reliability and cost, not agreement with reference answer. The self-evolution loop. Tasks first execute using the fixed block snapshot. After task finishes, its trajectory τi is projected to label-free record di = Abs(τi): task signature, resource decisions, tool sequence, process checks, failures, and available costs. This abstraction excludes answers, literal scene coordinates, and raw task content from the transferable state. For completed block Bb, let Db = {di : Bb}. Only then do the stores update: Pb+1 = Upolicy(Pb, Db), Lb+1 = Uskill(Lb, Db). (5) Here Upolicy consolidates condition-specific strategic records and statistics; Uskill updates procedural records and their availability. Equation 5 is state update, not gradient step. sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: We evaluate MMSI, MindCube, OmniSpatial, SpaceDG, and SAT on 1,000, 1,050, 1,533, 1,000, and 150 items, respectively [12, 19, 24, 28, 33]. We report accuracy, using mean relative accuracy (MRA) for numeric SpaceDG questions. SpaceDG uses fixed 1,000-item subset, and SAT uses fixed option order. The direct-answer baseline and SpatialBrain both use GPT-5.6-sol on the same items. Predictions are fixed before scoring; experience updates use neither reference answers nor future tasks. Table 1 includes foundation VLMs, spatially trained models, and agentic frameworks. It combines published results with our evaluations, so backbones and protocols vary across methods. These comparisons position the framework among available approaches, while the shared-backbone pair measures its gain over direct answers. Appendix gives evaluation settings and comparison details.

sections.title: 4.2 Main Results
sections.content: SpatialBrain improves on direct GPT-5.6-sol answers on four benchmarks and ties on SAT  (Table 1)  , raising the unweighted mean from 67.5 to 72.6. MindCube accounts for the largest gain, at 20.4 percentage points; the smaller changes on OmniSpatial and SpaceDG show that the benefit depends on the task setting. Categorylevel changes are mixed, including regressions on OmniSpatials egocentric questions and SpaceDGs distance and counting questions.

sections.content: Figure 4 breaks errors down by benchmark task type. On MindCube, errors decrease in all three categories, from 344 to 130 overall, 62.2% reduction. On MMSI, SpatialBrain makes 33 fewer errors overall, but the direction of change varies: positional and attribute errors decrease, with no uniform reduction across all task types. sections.title: 5.1 Component Analysis
sections.content: We compare SpatialBrain with three component-removal configurations. w/o Skill Library removes seed and accumulated skills, retrieval, hints, macros, and induction while retaining primitive tools. w/o 3DFusionMemory disables scene-graph construction and access, including queries inside skills and memory-based answer checks. w/o SpatialCognition replaces task-specific analysis and adaptive routing with generic controller. Figure 6 summarizes the MindCube configurations on all 1,050 items. SpatialBrain scores 87.6, compared with 76.7 without the Skill Library, 75.2 without 3DFusionMemory, 78.8 without SpatialCognition, and 67.2 for direct answers. The component-removal gaps are larger on Among and Around than on Rotation. Missing and refused answers count as wrong throughout. Appendices and B.3 report the settings and answer availability. Appendix B.4 reports the earlier MMSI component study (Figure A2).

Across five GPT-5.6-sol evaluation streams, saved 3D objects occur in 50.6% of MMSI tasks and 37.5% of SpaceDG tasks, compared with 21.0%, 29.2%, and 18.0% for MindCube, OmniSpatial, and SAT (Appendix B.1). This variation reflects which inputs produce spatial state; coverage does not measure retrieval or geometric accuracy.

sections.title: 5.3 Experience and Skill Coverage
sections.content: Figure 7 tracks the breadth of stored experience across five independent GPT-5.6-sol streams. Task coverage counts distinct task signatures with experience records; skill coverage counts existing seed skill IDs referenced by those records, not newly generated programs. MMSI reaches 165 task signatures and 24 seed skills, while MindCube reaches 12 and 10. On MMSI, task coverage continues to grow after skill coverage begins to plateau: further experience extends the recorded task conditions without comparable increase in distinct referenced skills. Appendix B.2 separately measures how often earlier experience reaches subsequent tasks in the executable 8 Figure 7 Test-time experience and seed-skill coverage. (a) Distinct task signatures with stored experience. (b) Distinct seed skills referenced by that experience. Each curve spans the benchmarks full evaluation scope (Section 4.1). configuration. Individual trajectories show how experience changes route or skill recommendation (Appendix C.3). An earlier GPT-5.5 hint-retrieval experiment also logged partial sequence alignment, but did not improve aggregate accuracy or cost (Appendix B.6). The relevant contrast for update benefits is an initial-frozen control with the same resources and starting experience. Limitations. Published baselines differ in protocols and serving precision, and our SAT evaluation fixes option order. Removing 3DFusionMemory also removes memory-based answer checks, so it does not isolate storage alone. The experience curves and selected trajectories establish accumulation and use, not general improvement from self-evolution. Perception and geometry errors also remain imperfectly calibrated. Matched evaluations should measure both answer quality and the full cost of acquiring and using experience.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: SpatialBrain separates evidence about the current scene from reusable spatial computation and experience about when and how to use it. 3DFusionMemory, the Spatial Skill Library, and Spatial Cognition implement these roles around fixed vision-language backbone. Completed trajectories update external experience between task blocks, making self-evolution an inspectable change in the resources and decisions available to later tasks. The complete framework improves on direct answers on four of five benchmarks and ties on the fifth.

sections.title: B Supplementary Analyses
sections.content: The Direct/SpatialBrain error comparisons use the reported main-table predictions. The five-stream memory and experience coverage analyses use the earlier GPT-5.6-sol test-time batch (Appendix A). The multi-view illustration in Figure 3 comes from separate saved MMSI scene in the strict-component run. The experienceexposure counts in Appendix B.2 use the later executable configuration on full MMSI and MindCube. Counts are reported separately for each evaluation batch. B.1 3DFusionMemory Coverage Figure A1 counts tasks with nonempty saved 3D objects and spatial relations. Object and relation coverage overlap, so the left panel plots them separately. The right panel partitions each evaluation set into snapshots with 3D objects, snapshots without 3D objects, and missing snapshots. The last category is unknown rather than an observed empty memory. Every percentage uses the full evaluation denominator, including 1,000 sampled SpaceDG items. Figure A1 Stored spatial evidence across benchmarks. (a) Tasks with 3D objects or relations. (b) Snapshot availability and 3D-object presence. Coverage measures stored state, not retrieval or answer correctness. There are 506/220/448/375/27 tasks with 3D objects and 257/146/201/213/17 with relations on MMSI/MindCube/OmniSpatial/SpaceDG/SAT. Missing snapshots number 33/0/30/7/1. Multiple camera states occur in 710/496/0/574/0 tasks, respectively. MMSI and SpaceDG show higher object and relation coverage than the other streams, but coverage does not follow universal 3D-versus-2D split. The example in Figure 3 illustrates complementary view support: the displayed views support two, three, and four of its five 3D objects, and their union covers all five. This describes observed support, not object recall against ground truth. B.2 Experience Coverage and Subsequent Exposure Beyond the stored coverage in Figure 7, we measure exposure to earlier experience in the executable configuration on complete MMSI and MindCube streams. MMSI forms 18 experience records, six of which become available; MindCube forms five, with three available. These are condition-specific resource-use records, not new algorithms. Nonempty experience from an earlier committed state reaches 231 of 1,000 MMSI tasks and 212 of 1,050 MindCube tasks. Matching the injected record IDs to each targets input state verifies that their supporting events precede the target block. These exposure counts establish delivery to the reasoner, not successful execution or an improvement in answers. 15 B.3 Input-Derived Reasoning Categories The radar in Figure 4 uses input-derived task signatures recorded by the label-blind router, with the same label assigned to every methods response for each item. We group relation as Relations; motion and rotation as Motion/rotation; route sequence as Sequential reasoning; visual measurement, count, diagram geometry, and depth as Measurement; and attribute, appearance, affordance, and spatial physics as Other attributes/actions. This mapping was fixed before aggregating outcomes and retains every item. Direct responses often lack the traces needed to diagnose the cause of wrong answer. Table A2 reports the category counts and pooled error rates used in the radar. Table A2 Errors within input-derived categories. Top: Direct/SpatialBrain wrong-answer counts, with category size in parentheses. Bottom: pooled error rates (%) for all radar curves. Motion/rotation improves mainly on MindCube; sequential reasoning regresses on MMSI, and its Other group is unchanged. Measurement has no MindCube items under this signature taxonomy. The component curves come from the later executable implementation and include its own Full reference. On MindCube/MMSI, this Full makes 253/543 errors, compared with 238/500 without the Skill library and 260/521 without 3DFusionMemory. The gap to main-table SpatialBrain also includes implementation changes and cannot isolate components contribution. MindCubes component runs passed their runtime checks; the MMSI curves are independently scored complete predictions whose runtime audits remain unverified. Blank answers count as errors throughout. 16 B.4 MMSI Component Comparison This earlier GPT-5.6-sol study compares Full with three removal configurations on the same 1,000 MMSI items (Figure A2). It is separate from the main-table comparison. Full makes 487 errors, versus 505/519/522 for Skill/Memory/Cognition removal. Errors differ most on positional questions; multi-step errors are unchanged by memory removal. The configurations were not verified as complete removals, and unanswered items account for part of the gaps (Appendix A). Figure A2 MMSI component errors by task family. Earlier component configurations on all 1,000 items. Bars count wrong answers, including unanswered questions. The four families partition the evaluation set; configuration and answer-availability differences are detailed in Appendix A. B.5 MMSI Errors by Task Type Figure A3 compares Direct and SpatialBrain on all 1,000 MMSI items and eleven task types. Direct makes 462 errors and SpatialBrain makes 429, with 199 corrections and 166 reversals. Cameraobject errors decrease from 53 to 24 and appearance errors from 39 to 25, whereas multi-step errors increase from 83 to 94. Regionregion errors are unchanged. Figure A3 MMSI errors by task type. Direct GPT-5.6-sol answers and SpatialBrain on all 1,000 items. Each rate divides wrong answers by the number of items in that type. Lower is better. B.6 Earlier Retrieval and Sequence Alignment In an earlier GPT-5.5 experiment, 500 MMSI source tasks produce 81 procedural records across 36 taskpath families and 16 capability skeletons. Among 500 disjoint target tasks, 332 are eligible for retrieval: 122 retrieve record (36.7%) and 59 execute partially matching tool sequence (17.8%). Partial alignment requires ordered overlap covering at least half of retrieved sequence; it occurs in 48.4% of tasks with retrieved records. This analysis does not count newly generated skills or measure answer improvements. The experiment did not improve aggregate accuracy or cost. It is separate from the full executable-cohort exposure counts in Appendix B.2.

sections.title: C Qualitative Analysis and Visualizations
sections.content: We group the examples by their role in spatial reasoning: 3DFusionMemory for grounding, the Skill Library for reusable procedures, and SpatialCognition for experience-guided resource choices. Teal, purple, and amber boxes identify these three groups; blue-gray boxes show additional tool-based trajectories. Component / box color Examples (MMSI IDs) 3DFusionMemory / teal Atlas exposure and spatial verification: 9, 206; multi-view representations: 297, 861. Successful skill returns and answer correction: 32, 42. Skill Library / purple SpatialCognition / amber Experience-guided routing: 748; adaptive skill selection: 348. Supporting traces / blue-gray Coordinate and temporal reasoning: 18, 82; shorter paths and fallback: 289, 880; boundary cases: 715, 416. Case selection. The ten detailed trajectories and two compact boundary cases come from the 1,000-item MMSI evaluations with GPT-5.6-sol. Seven show an incorrect Direct answer and correct SpatialBrain answer. We selected these examples after scoring to explain distinct execution paths; they are not representative of the full set, which has 199 corrections and 166 reverse outcomes. Overall scores are 53.8% for Direct, 57.4% for the fixed-policy control, and 57.1% for SpatialBrain. The boxes show observed operations rather than isolated component effects; executing an existing skill is distinct from learning new one. The two memory visualizations illustrate saved spatial representations, independently of answer correctness. For the SpatialCognition cases, we checked that the cited experience precedes the target task and that the later resource choice follows that experience. Compute comparisons. Unless stated otherwise, compute comparisons use the fixed-policy control. Of 485 both-correct fixed-policy/SpatialBrain pairs, 480 have complete token records, 221 use fewer SpatialBrain tokens, and 71 also use fewer non-final top-level calls and less observed time. Of 372 both-correct Direct/SpatialBrain pairs, 371 have complete tokens and only MMSI 748 uses fewer SpatialBrain tokens; both paths use zero tools. Call counts include failed attempts and exclude final-answer generation; primitive calls inside skill are counted separately from top-level calls. Elapsed times are observational: concurrency and caches were not controlled. The evaluations used the same task IDs, model, and protocol, but exact image-byte identity could not be checked because per-run hashes were not recorded. 19 C.1 3DFusionMemory 3DFusionMemory: Cross-view Spatial Grounding MMSI 9 3DFusionMemory Answer Correction Question When you are going upstairs in the stairwell area, where is the food storage area located relative to you? A. In front B. Behind C. On the left D. On the right Image Image 2 Direct C. On the left SpatialBrain Incorrect 1. The coordinate check combines the two island observations after consistency check and uses the stove to define east. 3. The mural displacement has east = -0.360 and north = +0.432. Northwest The coordinate check combines the island observations; memory keeps them separate and does not override the answer. 21 Multi-view Support in 3DFusionMemory These two examples connect image detections to 3D anchors, camera poses, and supporting views. We selected them for visible geometry, without using answer correctness. The overhead inset shows the same state from second viewpoint, not later fusion step. Colored matrix cells indicate recorded view support, not independently verified object matches. All coordinates are unchanged; distance scales are not calibrated in meters. The additional overhead view separates the stored layout from the display camera perspective. 2/6 anchors have support in at least two views. Single-view support in other saved scenes. Four additional scene states distinguish shared-frame organization from repeated observations of the same object. MMSI 700 and 711 have 8 and 7 anchors, respectively; MindCube around/033d379d and around/0d8a8816 each have 5. None of these anchors has support in two or more views. In around/033d379d, all five anchors come from view 1 despite three retained camera poses. These states illustrate stored spatial layouts rather than repeated-observation fusion. 23 C.2 Spatial Skill Library These examples show how existing skills provide structured spatial outputs for answer generation. sections.title: Reasoning and Cost Boundaries
sections.content: Correct answers can coexist with an unsupported geometric shortcut or more expensive execution path. These cases distinguish answer correctness from the quality and cost of the supporting procedure. Boundary Case: Cross-view Height Comparison MMSI 715 Question Which is higher, the fabric on the left or the sink on the right? A. The same height B. The sink C. The fabric D. Sometimes the fabric is higher, sometimes the sink is higher Image 2 Image 1 B. The sink B. The sink Direct SpatialBrain Correct Correct The procedure detects the sink in image 1 and the fabric in image 2, then compares normalized box-center heights, 0.792 and 0.825. Its description invokes shared wall tiles as context, but the computation does not estimate cross-view alignment. Normalization alone does not establish common height reference across these views; the correct answer therefore does not validate this geometric shortcut. Both runs use the same memory-off/hint route. Fixed-policy control SpatialBrain: 64,712 58,586 tokens (9.5%), 3 3 non-final top-level calls, and 196.1 102.6 observed. Standalone Direct is also correct with 3,534 tokens. Boundary Case: Compute Trade-offs MMSI 416 Question This is set of photos took at home. In the last photo, in which direction is the exit area relative to me? A. front left B. back left C. front right D. back right Image 2 Image 1 A. front left A. front left Direct SpatialBrain Correct Correct Detect the exit, reconstruct both views, and project the exit into 3D. Its coordinates in the last camera frame are = 0.852, = +0.987, giving front left. This is an exploratory route with memory disabled. Fixed-policy control SpatialBrain: 123,214 111,609 tokens (9.4%), 4 5 non-final top-level calls, and 258.9 262.3 observed. Fewer tokens here do not imply fewer calls or shorter time.

sections.title: D Memory Fusion and Experience Updates
sections.content: D.1 Confidence-weighted Scene Fusion Reconstruction provides common scene frame. For matched object o, µo R3 is its current center and Wo its accumulated confidence weight. projection from view supplies center (cid:101)µo,v and weight wo,v: µ+ = Woµo + wo,v (cid:101)µo,v Wo + wo,v , + = Wo + wo,v. (A1) The superscript + denotes the updated state. The view-specific center is the confidence-weighted centroid of projected points, or their arithmetic mean if total confidence is zero; wo,v is their mean confidence. The first valid projection initializes the estimate. Equation A1 requires Wo + wo,v > 0. These weights express relative support, not calibrated probabilities. D.2 Conservative Strategy Admission In the executable configuration, consider one route or memory factor with default action a0 and alternative a. Statistics are conditioned on the task signature and use only earlier blocks. Eligibility requires min{na, na0 } nmin, Rupper ϵ, ncost = nu (u {a, a0}),

C upper
a
sections.content: (1 δ)C lower a0 . (A2) For action u, nu counts observations and ncost complete cost records; nmin is the minimum support. Incomplete costs cannot establish saving. Rupper is Wilson upper estimate of the process-violation rate, including unverified actions; ϵ is its tolerance. The cost bounds use the sample mean plus or minus 1.96 standard errors, with the lower bound floored at zero. δ [0, 1) is the required fractional saving. Thus equation A2 compares candidates upper cost with the defaults lower cost, not just two point estimates. The controller checks the specific context before broader task family; supported context-specific risk can veto broader recommendation. At each level it chooses the eligible alternative with the lowest upper cost, retaining the default if none qualifies. These are process-feedback gates, not correctness rewards or guarantees of answer accuracy. They describe the executable configuration, not every historical run in the paper. D.3 Learned and Fixed State The initial library, task-signature schema, tool interfaces, validation checks, and update rules are specified before evaluation. Experience changes support statistics, associations between task conditions and strategies, and procedural availability. The executable configuration can also compile and validate new procedures. Some failure-check text comes from predefined rules: observing failure adds its applicability and support, rather than inventing an unrestricted instruction. selected skill, an exposed hint, an executed procedure, verified return, and correct answer are distinct events. Process observations cannot establish answer correctness without the separate evaluation labels, which are not used by the update loop.
